title: Fitting a Parabola to Its Two Intercepts and Vertex
originalTopic: Determining a quadratic from graphical data points
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: A graphing tool's curve-fitting feature is handed the information that a parabola crosses the x-axis at x = 0 and x = 2 and has its vertex at (1, -1). Find its equation, and say how the answer would change if the vertex were (1, -2) instead.

steps.title: Start from the intercept form
steps.explanation: Knowing the two x-intercepts pins the quadratic up to one unknown stretch factor a.
steps.why: Intercept form automatically satisfies both given zeros, leaving a single parameter to fit.

steps.title: Use the vertex to fix a
steps.explanation: Substituting the vertex (1, -1) gives a = 1, so the equation is y = x(x - 2) = x^2 - 2x.
steps.why: One extra point determines the remaining degree of freedom in a quadratic, which is why three independent conditions are exactly what is needed.

steps.title: Check the fit on screen
steps.explanation: Plotting y = x^2 - 2x over a small window reproduces all three given points, confirming the algebra.
steps.why: Graphical verification catches sign and transcription errors that pure algebra can hide.

steps.title: Note the effect of a deeper vertex
steps.explanation: If the vertex is instead (1, -2), the same intercepts force a vertical stretch by 2, giving y = 2x(x - 2).
steps.why: This shows the leading coefficient is exactly what the depth of the vertex measures when the zeros are fixed.
